entry.hook: Mang Mountain Ghost King (邙山鬼王) is not a single dead man—he is the collective fury of nine dynasties of emperors and nobles, stitched together inside the skull of a grave robber who dared to dig where kings sleep. He did not become a king by conquest. He became one by swallowing the sleeping souls of a thousand years, and now he sits on a throne of bone in the dark heart of a necropolis, his own name long forgotten.

body.body_1:
邙山鬼王 (Mang Mountain Ghost King) / 真名不详 (True name unknown)  
在盗墓时被墓主人魂魄反噬杀死 (Killed by the tomb owner's vengeful spirit while grave-robbing)  
Era of Death: Eastern Han to Northern Wei Dynasties (approx. 2nd–6th century CE)  
Current Ghost Path Level: Gui Wang (Ghost King)  
Underworld Jurisdiction: Mang Mountain Necropolis (邙山陵墓群), a self-contained ghost domain over a hundred li square
body.body_2: The Mang Mountain Ghost King sits at the apex of the Gui Wang (Ghost King) stratum. He has existed for well over a millennium—his soul was trapped in the imperial tomb cluster of Mang Mountain shortly after his death, and he has never left. At this level, his form is a composite of thousands of devoured souls, each screaming with its own death. His Yin Qi is so dense that local Gang Feng (Cosmic Gale) bends around the mountain like water around a stone. He commands an army of ghost soldiers—the specters of ancient kings, generals, and ministers who once ruled the Central Plains—but inside his own consciousness, he endures the accumulated torment of every ruler he swallowed: their loneliness in death, their rage at betrayal, their grief over fallen dynasties. The Ghost King does not sleep, because sleep would mean letting the thousand voices take control.
body.body_3: The grave robber died in the dark. He had broken into a sealed royal tomb beneath Mang Mountain, expecting gold and jade. Instead, he found the tomb owner still present—a centuries-old Hun (ethereal soul) of a king, dense with accumulated Yin and unresolved resentment. The king’s spirit did not kill him instantly. It dragged him into the burial chamber and forced him to witness the king’s entire life: the campaigns, the feasts, the betrayals, the slow decay of power, and finally the loneliness of the sealed tomb as generation after generation of descendants forgot his name. The grave robber watched for what felt like days as the king’s memory played through his own mind. When it ended, the king’s hands closed around his throat. The last sensation the robber felt was the cold of the stone floor against his back as his own soul peeled away from his body. He had been dead for several minutes before he realized he was still conscious—and trapped in the same tomb, with the king's spirit now staring at him from the darkness.
body.body_4: His first shelter was the burial chamber itself. The stone walls and layers of earth above blocked the worst of the Celestial Gale, but the cold of the underworld seeped through every crack. For the first months, he existed in a state of pure terror, reliving his own death in loops. Then he understood the nature of the place: beneath Mang Mountain, the burial mounds of nine dynasties formed a vast Yin energy nexus. Thousands of royal souls lay dormant, their consciousness half-dissolved, held together by centuries of accumulated resentment and imperial dignity. They did not wander. They slept, dreaming of their former lives. The grave robber—now a Li Hun (departed soul) with nothing left to lose—began to consume them. The first was a minor prince of the Eastern Han. He swallowed the soul's remaining Yin, and with it, a flood of memories: a childhood in the palace, a failed coup, a slow poisoning. The grave robber’s own mind became a little less his own. But the Yin was sustaining, and he was no longer afraid of the wind. He kept eating.
body.body_5: After a century of feasting, the grave robber was no longer a single identity. He had consumed the souls of three emperors, seven princes, dozens of generals, and countless noble lords. Each added its layer: one emperor contributed the memory of building an empire, another contributed the taste of defeat. A general gave him the sensation of a spear piercing his gut; a concubine gave him the smell of burning incense in a sealed palace. He sat in the central tomb and tried to recall his own mother's face—but his mind offered up five different faces from five different lifetimes, and he could not tell which was real. He knew his own name for a while, then lost it. He kept only the title he gave himself: King of Mang Mountain. But he could no longer say whether he was the grave robber who chose to stay, or the first king he swallowed, dreaming that he was a thief. The distinction had dissolved.
body.body_6: By the Tang dynasty, the Mang Mountain Ghost King had reached full Gui Wang status. His domain extended over the entire mountain range, and his Yin Qi could swallow daylight for a li in any direction. He commanded an army of ghost soldiers, the reanimated specters of buried warriors, who stood in silent ranks beneath the hills. Yet in the deep night, when the moon was thin, the Ghost King would sit on his throne of petrified bone—a construct made from the splintered remains of a thousand coffins—and weep without knowing whose tears they were. The tears were a king's tears, and a thief's, and a father's, and a murderer's. He had long since surpassed the need to fear the Underworld's escorts; the few Niu Tou Ma Mian who ventured near his domain turned back at the boundary. But he did not attempt the Gui Xian (Ghost Immortal) path. He knew that the moment he tried to reverse Yin into Yang, the accumulated weight of a thousand kings would drag him down, and the Heavenly Thunder would find him before the first spark caught. He stayed a king. It was the only role left that felt like his own.
body.body_7: The Underworld has never formally processed the Mang Mountain Ghost King. He is not listed in the Sheng Si Bu (Book of Life and Death) under any known name—his original identity was erased long ago, and the devoured souls each have their own records in separate volumes. The Ten Yama Kings have discussed his case in council, but no judge has been willing to descend into his domain to retrieve him. The Karma Mirror would show a chaos of lifetimes, and the sentence would be meaningless. The River of Oblivion lies far below, but he has never approached it. He does not want to forget—not because he values his memories, but because the act of forgetting would be the final victory of a thousand kings over the thief who thought he could own them.
body.body_8: Relations with other paths are minimal. No Daoist immortal has successfully conducted a Chao Du (Soul Deliverance) ritual over the Mang Mountain ghost domain; the combined resentment of the buried royalty resists all incantations. Buddhist monks from nearby temples have occasionally attempted sutra recitations at the mountain's edge, but the Ghost King's Yin Qi dampens the sound before it reaches the deeper tombs. Local City Gods and Earth Gods treat the mountain as a forbidden zone, maintaining a silent truce: they do not enter, and the Ghost King does not expand his domain into populated areas. There are no records of Yao (妖) or Mo (魔) interference; the pure density of imperial Yin energy seems to repel other forms of contamination. As for mortals, the people of Luoyang have known for centuries not to dig too deep on Mang Mountain. They offer incense at the edges, not at the center.
body.body_9: The Mang Mountain Ghost King still rules his necropolis as of the present day. He has not been reclaimed by the Underworld, nor has he dissolved. He persists in a state of frozen stasis, conscious of every soul inside him, yet unable to let any of them go. The day may come when the accumulated karma of nine dynasties reaches a critical mass and he collapses into a chaos of pure Yin, scattering across the mountain like mist. But for now, he sits. He does not sleep, because when he does not consciously hold his identity together, the thousand kings begin to squabble over who gets to dream inside his skull. And so he stays awake, in the dark, under the weight of a mountain full of emperors, remembering nothing that was ever truly his.
body.body_10: The primary haunt is the entire Mang Mountain range itself, especially the area around the Northern Wei imperial tombs. Local folklore in Luoyang speaks of a "King of the Dead" who appears on stormy nights to travelers who stray too close to the ancient burial mounds. Some old villagers claim to have seen a figure in tattered grave-robber's clothes, crowned with a jade hairpin from a Han dynasty prince, standing on a ridge and watching the living pass. The most famous recorded encounter appears in the Tang dynasty zhi-guai collection *Ming Bao Ji*, where a band of tomb raiders was found dead at the entrance of a sealed tomb, their faces frozen in expressions of terror, and a single set of footprints—barefoot and too large for any man—led out of the tomb and into the hills. No trace of the footprints was ever found beyond the first ridge.
body.body_11: For a complete understanding of the ghost-path hierarchy, see the associated entry on Li Gui (Vengeful Spirits) and the process of identity dissolution through soul-consumption. The Mang Mountain Ghost King is a characteristic example of a Gui Wang whose domain is geophysically anchored—a type favored in Chinese folklore where the terrain itself serves as a Yin energy reservoir. His relationship with the Underworld is explored in the entry on the Ten Yama Kings and the limits of their jurisdictional reach. The lore of Mang Mountain's buried dynasties is recorded in the geographical treatise *Shui Jing Zhu* and the temple chronicle *Luo Yang Qie Lan Ji*.

guide.guide_1: Imagine you are standing on a hill in central China, just north of the ancient city of Luoyang. The grass is dry, the wind is thin, and beneath your feet—beneath about thirty feet of earth and stone—there are the remains of nine dynasties' worth of emperors, generals, ministers, and princesses. The Mang Mountain necropolis is the densest concentration of royal tombs in East Asia, and it has been a playground for grave robbers for almost two thousand years. Most of those robbers got rich and died in their beds. One of them did not. One of them broke into the wrong tomb, met a king who refused to be forgotten, and ended up not dead in the ordinary sense but dead in a way that kept him conscious, trapped, and slowly turning into something that the locals still talk about in hushed voices on the seventh month of the lunar calendar. His name? Nobody remembers. He calls himself the King of Mang Mountain. But he hasn't been sure whose name he's using for a very long time.
guide.guide_2: If you have ever read a Chinese ghost story, you have probably seen the trope: a tomb raider breaks into an imperial burial chamber, finds treasure, and gets cursed or killed by a guardian spirit. But the story of the Mang Mountain Ghost King is different in one crucial way. He did not become a ghost by supernatural decree or by violating a cosmic taboo. He simply refused to leave—and then discovered that the whole mountain was a pantry full of sleeping souls. The image of a ghost king commanding an army of spectral emperors is powerful, but the real horror is the cost. Every time you swallow a king's soul, you inherit his memory of the day his empire fell. Every time you swallow a general's soul, you feel the blade that killed him. By the time he had eaten a few hundred of them, the grave robber had ceased to be a person. He had become a living archive of every death that had ever occurred on that mountain. That is what the local folklore misses: the ghost king is not a villain. He is a tragedy of accumulated pain.
guide.guide_3: The moment of death for this grave robber was not a single, clean event. It was a process. When the tomb king's soul dragged him into the burial chamber and forced his own memories into the robber's mind, the robber experienced a complete biography in real time. He saw the king's birth, his crowning, his battles, his aging, his burial. By the time the king's hands closed around his throat, the robber had already lived an entire lifetime that was not his own. When his own soul left his body, he found himself standing beside the corpse of the king—except the king's soul was now sitting back in its sarcophagus, looking at him with something like satisfaction. The robber tried to run up the tunnel, but his feet left the ground. He floated. He was already a ghost. And the light at the tunnel's mouth was not daylight—it was starlight filtered through a foot of earth. He was trapped in the dark, with a dead king who was more alive than he was, and the first lesson of death in the Eastern universe hit him: you cannot touch anything, you cannot feel the wind on your face, you are alone in a way that no living person can understand, and the only company is the dead who may not want you there.
guide.guide_4: The Ghost King's survival strategy—if you can call it that—was the most brutal version of the ghost-path logic. In the Chinese cosmology, a ghost is held together by attachment. The deeper the attachment, the stronger the ghost. The grave robber had nothing left to hold onto except his terror of being alone in the dark. But Mang Mountain offered an alternative: every sealed tomb contained a soul that had been dormant for centuries, held together not by attachment to life but by the sheer weight of royal pride. These souls were not active. They were dreaming. And the robber learned that he could consume them. Imagine being so hungry that you eat the dreams of a dead emperor. Imagine the first mouthful of that dream: the taste of a victory feast, the sound of a hundred thousand troops cheering, the warmth of a throne on your back. And then imagine the next mouthful: the same emperor's death, the slow suffocation under silk pillows, the final thought of "I should have killed him first." That is what it means to grow strong as a ghost in this system. You get stronger, but you also get contaminated by every life you absorb. The grave robber ate hundreds of kings. He became a palimpsest of dynasties. And somewhere in that accretion, his own name dissolved into the static of ten thousand memories.
guide.guide_5: Most ghosts who reach the Gui Wang stage do so by consuming hundreds or thousands of ordinary souls. The Mang Mountain Ghost King is unusual because his diet was exclusively royal souls—each one dense with centuries of power, resentment, and the accumulated karma of an entire lineage. The result is a being whose power rivals that of a mid-ranking celestial god, but whose psychology is a battlefield. Every night, the kings he swallowed try to reassert themselves. One wants to launch a campaign against the Underworld. Another wants to restore the glory of the Eastern Han. A third just wants to die properly and be forgotten. The Ghost King has to suppress them all with sheer will, which is why he cannot sleep. Sleep would mean letting a Han emperor take the helm. Sleep would mean waking up as someone else. As for the Gui Xian path—the attempt to reverse death itself by generating pure Yang—he knows it is impossible for him. The accumulated Yin of a thousand royal souls is too heavy. The moment he tried to generate a single spark of Yang, the combined weight would collapse his form. He is a king precisely because he cannot be anything else. He is stuck at the top of a mountain of the dead, and the only way out is to forget everything—which he refuses to do, because forgetting would mean letting the kings win.
guide.guide_6: The Underworld's relationship with the Mang Mountain Ghost King is a fascinating case study in the limits of cosmic bureaucracy. In the standard model, every soul is supposed to pass through the Ten Yama Kings, have its karma weighed on the Nie Jing Tai, drink Meng Po's brew, and cross the River of Oblivion into a new life. But the Ghost King exists outside that system. He was never registered under his true name, and his devoured victims each have separate entries in the Book of Life and Death. The Underworld's judges have discussed the case—the *Yan Luo Wang* are not ignorant of his existence—but they have not dispatched a retrieval squad. Why? Because to process him would require untangling a millennium of soul-addition, separating each king's karma from the thief's original record, and that would take more time and energy than the Underworld is willing to spend on a ghost who is not actively threatening the fabric of reincarnation. So he remains, a permanent exception, a rogue node in the cosmic network. It is not a mercy. It is simply efficiency. The Underworld does not punish or forgive; it processes. And the Mang Mountain Ghost King is simply too complex to process.
guide.guide_7: Let me leave you with a thought. The Mang Mountain Ghost King is a story about memory and identity—about what happens when you consume so many lives that you can no longer remember your own. But it is also a story about the opposite: the desperate, heartbreaking refusal to forget. The Ghost King could end his suffering at any moment. He could walk into the River of Oblivion, drink the water, and let his memories dissolve. He would be reborn as a new baby, perhaps, with a clean slate. But he will not do it. Because forgetting means that the thousand kings he swallowed will have won. They will have erased the thief who dared to steal from them, and left no trace of his existence. So he stays awake, in the dark, under a mountain of emperors, holding onto an identity that is no longer even his own. Is he a tragic figure? Yes. Is he a monster? Also yes. But the deepest lesson of the ghost path in Chinese cosmology is this: death does not free you from the burden of being someone. It only removes the distractions. The Mang Mountain Ghost King is what happens when you refuse to let go of yourself—even when yourself has become a crowd. The silence of that tomb is the sound of a thousand kings screaming, and one thief listening, and neither side willing to stop.

lore_entries.description: A mountain range near Luoyang, China, containing the densest concentration of imperial tombs from nine dynasties; a major Yin-energy nexus in Eastern cosmology.
A ghost who has consumed thousands of other souls, attaining immense power but losing individual identity; commands legions of lesser ghosts.
The specific type of Yin energy accumulated by buried emperors and nobles, denser and more resistant to dissipation than ordinary ghostly Yin.
A self-contained ghost territory that has become a permanent Yin-energy pocket, resisting the pull of the Underworld.
A 6th-century Chinese geographical text by Li Daoyuan that describes the rivers of China, including references to the Mang Mountain tombs.
A 6th-century Buddhist chronicle documenting temples and tombs in Luoyang, a key source for Mang Mountain necropolis lore.
A Tang dynasty collection of Buddhist miracle tales featuring ghost encounters, including tomb-robbing incidents at Mang Mountain.

faq_entries.question: Is the Mang Mountain Ghost King a real historical figure?
faq_entries.answer: No historical record names the individual; he is a composite folk figure built from centuries of grave-robbing legends and the actual geography of the Mang Mountain necropolis.

faq_entries.question: Why did the Underworld not retrieve him?
faq_entries.answer: His soul was never properly registered, and the complexity of untangling the karma of a thousand devoured kings made him a low-priority case for the Underworld's bureaucracy.

faq_entries.question: Can he ever escape his ghost state?
faq_entries.answer: Theoretically he could attempt the Gui Xian path (reverse Yin to Yang), but the accumulated weight of royal souls makes it nearly impossible. He could also choose to cross the River of Oblivion, but refuses out of attachment to what remains of his identity.

faq_entries.question: What powers does he have?
faq_entries.answer: He commands an army of ghost soldiers (specters of buried kings and generals), can extend his Yin domain to swallow daylight, and is immune to standard soul-escort tactics. His true power is territorial: he rules a self-contained ghost realm.

faq_entries.question: Are there any real-world haunted sites associated with him?
faq_entries.answer: The entire Mang Mountain range is considered haunted in local folklore; specific burial mounds near the Northern Wei emperor tombs are said to be his primary seat.
